They watched as the gap of dark, churning water widened; they watched as the figure of Henry, waving from the railing, grew smaller and less distinct; they watched until the vessel, catching the wind in its great white sheets, rounded a bend in the river and was lost to sight. And through it all, Thomas Ashworth stood as still and silent as a man of stone, his arm yet linked in Mr. Finch’s, though the need for its support was long past.

“Well,” said Mr. Finch at last, breaking the spell with a sigh that was half business and half genuine regret. “And so it is done. The Americas are a long way off, to be sure; but six months, in the course of a life, is but a brief chapter. He is a fine young man, a very fine young man.”

“He is,” agreed Mrs. Gable, turning her sharp gaze from the empty stretch of river to the face of the brother who remained. “And he has left his heart in good keeping, one hopes.”

This remark, pointed though it was, drew no response from Thomas. He seemed not to have heard it. His eyes, which had followed the ship, now stared at the vacant water with a fixed and hollow look, as though he saw not the bustling river traffic but some dreadful spectacle from his own mind.

“Come, my boy,” said Mr. Finch, giving the arm a gentle squeeze. “The air grows chill. The carriage is waiting to return us to a warm fire and, I daresay, a glass of something to fortify the spirits. Business must go on, you know; business must always go on.”

Thomas allowed himself to be led away, his steps mechanical, his face a mask of polite composure that failed utterly to conceal the profound disturbance within. To the concerned glance of Mr. Finch, it seemed as if the young man had erected a wall around himself, a wall of such perfect and chilling smoothness that no friendly voice could find purchase upon it.

The carriage ride back to the City was a thing of peculiar silence. Mr. Finch, after one or two failed attempts to draw Thomas into a conversation about shipping schedules and rates of exchange, fell into a troubled quiet, his brow furrowed with a concern that was far from commercial. Mrs. Gable, seated opposite, folded her hands in her lap and observed Thomas with an unwavering scrutiny, her expression a mixture of exasperation and a deep, grudging sympathy. She noted how his hands lay clenched in his lap, the knuckles showing white; she noted how his gaze was fixed upon the passing turmoil of the London streets, yet seemed to register nothing of it. It was the look of a man who had been carried to the very edge of a precipice and been forced to look down.

When they arrived back at the offices of Finch and Son, the familiar smell of paper and ink and dry dust seemed to have no effect on Thomas’s abstraction. He walked to his own desk in the outer office, the one he shared with his brother, and sat down in his customary chair. But he did not reach for the day’s correspondence, nor did he open the ledger that lay waiting for his attention. He simply sat, his hands resting on the desk before him, his eyes looking at the wall.

“Now then,” said Mr. Finch, bustling in with an air of manufactured cheerfulness. “A busy day awaits us. I have that matter of the Northern consignment to… Thomas? My dear boy?”

There was no answer. It was as if the Thomas Ashworth who kept the books with such meticulous care had departed on the ship with his brother, leaving only this pale, unseeing shell behind.

“Leave him be,” said Mrs. Gable in a low, firm voice from the doorway. “Can you not see he is unwell? Let him sit. The world will not end if a column of figures goes un-added for an hour.”

The hour stretched into the remainder of the afternoon. Clerks came and went, their footsteps softened as they passed the still figure at the desk. Messages were delivered, and Mr. Finch dealt with them himself, his usual briskness tempered by frequent, anxious glances towards his charge. Through it all, Thomas did not move, save for the slow, regular rise and fall of his chest.

As dusk began to gather in the narrow street outside, a change came over him. With a slow, deliberate motion, as of a man in a trance, he reached into a drawer of his desk and brought out, not the current ledgers of Finch and Son, but a small, bound book, its leather cover worn and faded. He took out a fresh nib, fixed it to a holder, opened a pot of ink, and began to write.

Mr. Finch and Mrs. Gable, watching from the doorway of the inner office, drew closer. He was not making entries of any known transaction. He was not composing letters. He was, with an air of intense and desperate concentration, filling the pages of the little book with columns of figures. They were neat, perfectly formed, and arranged with the faultless precision of a master clerk. But they were meaningless. They were numbers without names, sums without substance, a phantom accounting of a phantom enterprise. He would fill a page, blot it with the greatest care, turn it, and begin the next, his pen scratching with a steady, relentless rhythm in the deepening twilight.

“What is he doing?” whispered Mr. Finch, his face a picture of bewilderment. “This is not our work. I do not recognise that book.”

“He is doing what he knows,” Mrs. Gable answered, her voice uncharacteristically soft. “When the mind is in turmoil, the hands seek a familiar task. It is a kind of anchor.”

But as the days that followed were to prove, it was not an anchor so much as a descent. For nine full days, Thomas Ashworth lived in this waking dream. He rose at his usual hour, dressed with his usual neatness, and came to the office. But once there, he would take out his little book and his pen, and the day would be consumed in the silent, furious industry of his phantom accounting. He spoke to no one, and seemed to hear no one who spoke to him. He took the food Mrs. Gable placed before him, eating without seeming to taste, his eyes fixed upon his work. At night, Mr. Finch would have to lead him home, and in the stillness of the house, they could sometimes hear the faint, persistent scratching of his pen continuing late into the night.

Mr. Finch, in his distress, sought out young Finch, his son. “You were the last to speak with him alone,” the old man said, his voice pleading. “Before Henry left. What passed between you? What did you tell him that could have wrought such a terrible change?”

Young Finch, a sober and responsible man himself, grew pale. “Father, I gave my word. It was a matter of the gravest confidence, concerning… concerning a past debt. I cannot break my word. I can only say that the knowledge was necessary, for his own protection and for Henry’s. I had no idea… I could not have foreseen this.”

“A debt?” Mr. Finch repeated, baffled. “The boys have no debts but those I am aware of. Their father left them clear.”

“A debt of a different kind,” was all his son would say, and Mr. Finch was left with a mystery that was darker and more troubling than before.

The vigil was kept by the two old friends, a strange echo of that other vigil they had once kept over two orphaned boys. Mr. Finch, whose world was built on the solid foundations of contracts and balances, found himself adrift in a sea of uncertainty. He would sit for hours in his office, the door ajar, listening to the ceaseless scratch of Thomas’s pen, his own work forgotten. He felt as if the dependable machinery of his world had slipped a cog, and he knew not how to set it right.

Mrs. Gable, for her part, was a rock of formidable practicality. She ensured that Thomas was fed, that his fire was lit, that his linen was clean. She guarded him from the curious eyes of the other clerks with a ferocity that permitted no questions. But in the quiet moments, when she looked at the young man’s bent head and the desperate, mechanical motion of his hand, her own stern composure would falter, and her face would soften with a sorrow and a fear that she would have died rather than admit.

On the morning of the tenth day, a bright, clear Sunday, a breaking point was reached. The scratching had gone on since dawn, more rapid and more frantic than before. The little book was almost full. Mrs. Gable, entering the room with a breakfast tray, stood and watched him for a full minute. He did not look up. His face was gaunt, his eyes ringed with dark shadows, and a feverish intensity burned in them. He was, she saw with a sudden, chilling certainty, consuming himself.

With a motion as swift and decided as the closing of a ledger, she walked to the desk, took the pen from his unresisting fingers, and closed the little book.

Thomas looked up, his eyes slowly coming into focus, as if seeing her for the first time in over a week. A look of immense, desolate confusion passed over his features. He looked at the closed book, at his ink-stained fingers, and then around the quiet room, as though waking in a strange land.

“Mrs. Gable?” he said, his voice a dry, unused whisper.

“Yes, Thomas,” she said, her own voice more gentle than he had ever heard it. “It is Sunday. A day of rest. Your work is done.”

He stared at the book, and a tremor ran through him, a deep, shuddering tremor of returning consciousness. He covered his face with his hands, and for the first time since this strange malady had befallen him, a sound escaped his lips; a low, ragged sob of pure exhaustion and despair.

Later that day, when Thomas was resting, pale but lucid, in an armchair by the fire, Mr. Finch approached the matter with the same delicate diplomacy he might use with a failing but important client. He sat opposite the young man, clearing his throat in his usual, business-like way.

“My dear Thomas,” he began, “I am an old man, and a man of business. I do not pretend to understand matters of the mind, or the… the afflictions that may befall it. But as your friend, and as one who holds you and your brother in the highest affection, I must speak.”

Thomas looked at him, his expression guarded but attentive.

“For these past nine days,” Mr. Finch continued, “you have been… not yourself. You have been engaged in a labour,” he gestured towards the desk where the little book still lay, “that has caused great distress to you, and to those who care for you. It is like the work of a man in a fever, who believes he is performing a vital task, but is only wearing away his own strength.”

He paused, choosing his words with care. “I do not ask for the cause. I have no right. The confidence that passed between you and my son is your own. But I must ask you, for your own sake, and for the sake of your brother Henry, to whom we have a duty of care in his absence; do you believe you are recovered from this… this spell of industry?”

Thomas was silent for a long moment, his gaze directed into the flames. “I believe so,” he said at last, his voice low. “I feel as though I have returned from a very long and arduous journey.”

“And the tools of that journey?” Mr. Finch asked gently, his eyes indicating the book and pen. “The work that you performed. Is it a comfort to you to have it by you? Or is it, perhaps, a reminder of the fever you would wish to forget?”

Another silence. The only sound was the crackle of the fire and the distant cry of a vendor in the street.

“It is a reminder,” Thomas said, so quietly he could barely be heard. “A reminder of a dark place I have no wish to visit again.”

“Then,” said Mr. Finch, leaning forward, his manner full of a paternal earnestness, “as your friend and your banker, in a manner of speaking, might I propose a course of action? Let us treat this matter as we would a bad debt, an account that is closed and can bring no profit. Let us dispose of the evidence. Let us burn the book.”

Thomas’s eyes widened slightly, and he looked from Mr. Finch’s sincere face to the small, worn volume on the desk. It contained, he knew, nothing but nonsense. And yet, it was the nonsense that had consumed nine days of his life, the tangible record of his descent into the abyss. He had a sudden, morbid urge to keep it, to hide it away as a secret penance.

But then he looked back at Mr. Finch, at the genuine, unwavering kindness in the old man’s eyes. He thought of Henry, far away on the ocean, trusting in the life he had left behind. He thought of the promise he had made to young Finch, a promise that had cost him so dearly. To keep the book would be to keep the illness alive.

He gave a slow, deliberate nod. “Yes,” he said, his voice gaining a little of its former strength. “Let us dispose of it. Let us burn it, and speak of it no more.”

With a solemnity befitting the occasion, Mr. Finch took the little book, and the pen that had filled its pages, and laid them in the heart of the fire. The dry paper and leather caught at once, curling, blackening, the columns of phantom figures glowing red for a moment before dissolving into a flutter of grey ash. They sat together in silence and watched it burn, until nothing at all remained, and the only account left was the unwritten one, locked away in the quiet, resolute, and guarded chambers of Thomas Ashworth’s memory.

And downstairs, the friends laid their plans, preparing to do battle with an enemy they could not see, for the soul of a man who was lost in the prison of his own mind. The shadows in the little house were deep that night, and the dawn was a long way off.

“He knew,” said Miss Pross, without looking up from her knitting. Her voice was sharp, and cut through the melancholy of the room. “He knew it was coming. The morning of the wedding. When you and he were alone in that room, Mr. Darnay.” It was not a question, but a statement of fact.

Charles stopped his pacing and looked at her. He remembered the Doctor’s deathly pallor when they had emerged, the fleeting look of dread Mr. Lorry had observed. He had believed it to be the natural anxiety of a father giving away his only child. Now, he saw it in a new and terrible light.

His mind, already in a fragile state, had borne the shock for as long as it could; it had held together through the ceremony, through the farewells, through three days of feigned normality. And then, it had shattered.

“It is my fault,” Charles said, sinking into a chair and burying his face in his hands. “I have done this. I have brought the curse of my family upon this house.”

“Nonsense!” snapped Miss Pross, her loyalty to Lucie extending, by necessity, to Lucie’s husband. “You did as he asked. You kept your promise. The fault lies with those devils, your relations, not with you. The question is not whose fault it is, but what is to be done.”

Her practical, if brusque, assessment seemed to clear the air. Mr. Lorry straightened up, once more the man of business facing a difficult account.

“She is right,” he said. “Recrimination is a luxury we cannot afford. The damage is done. Our task now is to effect the repairs. I propose a course of action. Tomorrow, I will speak with him. Not as a friend, not as a family member, but on a matter of professional opinion.”

He looked from Charles to Miss Pross, his expression growing more resolute. “I will present him with a hypothetical case. A dear friend of mine whose mind has been… disturbed. It was a daring stratagem, one fraught with peril. It sought to pit the two sides of the Doctor’s personality against one another; to use the rational, learned physician to diagnose and defeat the broken prisoner. For a long moment, silence reigned in the room as Charles and Miss Pross considered the plan. It was delicate, it was dangerous, and it was all they had.

“Do it,” said Charles, looking up, a flicker of hope in his eyes. “It may be our only chance to bring him back to us, without his even knowing he has been away.”

And so, upstairs, the daughter watched over the father, her love a constant, silent plea against the darkness. And downstairs, the friends laid their plans, preparing to do battle with an enemy they could not see, for the soul of a man who was lost in the prison of his own mind. The shadows in the little house were deep that night, and the dawn was a long way off.

“My dear Lucie, Doctor, Charles,” he began, his voice strained, “I bring news. Extraordinary news. From Paris.”

“Is it bad news?” she asked.

The people have stormed it. It has been taken.”

He sat perfectly upright in his chair, his hands gripping the arms, his face a mask of shocking whiteness. Not a muscle twitched, but all the colour had drained from his lips, and his eyes, fixed on some point beyond the wall, were wide with a resurrected horror. It was the face of a man who sees a ghost; a ghost not of a person, but of a place, a place of stone and darkness and despair.

“My father!” cried Lucie, rushing to his side. “Father, are you ill?”

He did not seem to hear her. He did not seem to see her. His gaze was fixed, his breathing shallow. The collected and calm manner, the mastery he had held for so long, had not broken, but it had become a thing of terrible, rigid tension, like a wire stretched to its absolute limit.

Charles and Mr. Lorry exchanged a look of pure terror. The sound they had both dreaded, the echo of the shoemaker’s hammer, was not in the room, but they could feel its rhythm in the frantic beating of their own hearts. The unseen assailant, the bitter waters of captivity, which he had held at bay for so long, were rising again, summoned from the depths by the fall of the very stones that had been their source. The walls of the Bastille had fallen in Paris; but in the quiet room in Soho, the walls of a mind, so carefully rebuilt, were being assailed anew by the clamour and the chaos of their collapse. The fortress of their peace had been breached at last.
